issues.issue: The subsection imposes a notice duty with no time limit, whereas Section 2.3(a) fixes a deadline for notice of the same schedule changes. The overlap raises which timing rule governs the Auction Agent's notice to BD.

"Take such other action as is required of BD pursuant to the Settlement Procedures" is an open-ended catch-all appended to a specific notice duty, with its content living in an incorporated document. Its reach is left to the Settlement Procedures rather than stated.

The Fee Rate "may be adjusted from time to time with the approval of the Company upon a written request of the Broker-Dealer", which does not say whether the Company may withhold approval at will or must act reasonably, nor when an adjustment takes effect. The adjustment mechanism is therefore incomplete on its face.

The fee formula distinguishes the case where "an Auction was not held" from one where an Auction was held, but says nothing about an Auction that is held and fails; whether BD earns the fee on failed auctions turns on that gap. "Deemed to be the subject of a Hold Order" likewise depends on incorporated material.

The proviso refers to the definition of "Broker-Dealer" "contained in the Series 2004 Auction Bonds", while Section 2.1(c) locates that definition in the Indenture. The two cross-references point to different documents for the same defined term.

The Bond Insurer is given a "right to pay" the fee with no statement of when the right arises, whether payment discharges the Company, or what subrogation follows. The single sentence leaves the consequence of the Insurer's payment unaddressed.

BD must "promptly deliver such funds to the party entitled to receive such funds" when its customer fails, without identifying that party or capping the obligation. Whether this makes BD a guarantor of its customers' settlement is a real question on these words.

The Auction Agent is said to act "solely as agent of the Trustee", yet under the preamble the Auction Agent and the Trustee are the same entity, Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. Reading the no-duty disclaimer alongside that identity requires construction.

Duties are limited to those "expressly set forth herein, or expressly incorporated herein by reference pursuant to Section 2.1(b)", but 2.1(b) incorporates the entire Auction and Settlement Procedures, so the express-duties limit absorbs a large external body of obligations. Whether that leaves the limitation any work is a whole-instrument point.

The first sentence excuses liability absent "negligence or misconduct", while the second excuses good-faith errors of judgment unless the Auction Agent was negligent in ascertaining the facts — two overlapping standards in one subsection. Which governs an alleged bad judgment is not settled by the text.

The subsection cross-refers to "Section 3.2(d) hereof" for acting through agents and attorneys, a section that does not appear in the executed instrument. A missing referent invites construction of the whole limitation.

Clause (ii) lets the Auction Agent decline legal action that "might, in its judgment, involve any expense or liability" unless given "indemnity satisfactory to the Auction Agent", both wholly subjective tests. How far that discretion goes is open.

The excuse is for "circumstances beyond its reasonable control, including without limitation" a list of physical calamities, and the list ends abruptly with no closing catch-all; whether market or systemic events fall within it is the ejusdem generis question. The truncated list makes the reach of the general phrase harder to fix.

Telecopied notices are effective "when such telecopy is transmitted" regardless of receipt, and the final sentence requires signature authority only for BD and the Auction Agent, saying nothing about the Company. The omission leaves who may give the Company's notices unaddressed.

The integration clause sweeps in "the other agreements and instruments executed and delivered in connection with the issuance of the Series 2004 Auction Bonds" without identifying them, so the boundary of the integrated whole is undefined. "Relating to the subject matter hereof" carries the same open edge.

The clause makes the agreement enforceable by, and beneficial to, only the Auction Agent, the Bond Insurer and BD "other than the rights expressly granted to the Issuer herein", omitting the Company entirely. Whether a signatory can be written out of its own contract's benefit is exactly the kind of question a court decides.

The Company is a named party in the preamble with operative rights and duties — it directs schedule changes under Section 2.3(a), may bar own-account Bids under 2.1(d), and pays the fee under 2.5 — yet Section 5.5 gives it no right or remedy. That is a direct incoherence with those provisions.

Amendment requires the written consent of the Issuer and the Bond Insurer, neither of whom is a party under the preamble, and the Issuer's only stake is the limited rights preserved by Section 5.5. Whether non-parties' consent is a true condition is a cross-provision question.

The anti-waiver sentence protects rights only "with respect to any subsequent breach", which by negative implication may concede waiver as to the breach not acted upon. That expressio unius reading is available on the words.

The clause designates "the United States District Court in the County of New York", a court that does not exist — New York County lies in the Southern District — so whether it names a federal court, state courts in that county, or is unenforceable is genuinely open. It also does not say in terms that the chosen forum is exclusive despite "shall be brought".

The clause binds "the parties" to litigate only in New York, yet Section 5.5 denies the Company (a signatory) any right or remedy under the agreement; whether the Company is bound by a forum clause in a contract it cannot enforce is a cross-provision problem. The point turns on reading 5.9 with 5.5.

The no-implied-duties shield is written for the Company alone and reaches across three instruments (this agreement, the Indenture and the Auction Agreement), which could be read to negate the covenant of good faith in the Company's exercise of its discretions. The one-sided drafting is the source of the doubt.
